title: Letters and sounds
intro: Turkmen is written in a Latin alphabet of 30 letters, and it is written the way it sounds: one letter, one sound. This unit goes through the letters, the few sounds an English speaker has to learn, the long vowels that spelling doesn't show, and the shape of a Turkmen sentence. There is no audio in this course, so every sound is described with English words you already know.

blocks.text: Here is the alphabet in order. Most letters look and sound much as they do in English. Eight carry a mark: *ä, ç, ž, ň, ö, ş, ü, ý*. Each of them is a letter of its own, with its own place in the alphabet, not a decoration on another one.

blocks.text: Notice where the marked letters sit: *ä* after *e*, *ž* after *j*, *ň* after *n*, *ö* after *o*, *ş* after *s*, *ü* after *u*, *ý* after *y*. Dictionaries follow this order, so *ýok* comes after every word in *y*.

There is no c, q, v or x. Words borrowed from other languages are respelled with Turkmen letters: *Kanada* (Canada), *telewizor* (television), *kompýuter* (computer). Foreign names keep their own spelling only in English text.
Capitals work as in English: a sentence and a name start with one (*Salam!*, *Aýna*, *Aşgabat*). The marked letters have capitals too: *Ä, Ç, Ž, Ň, Ö, Ş, Ü, Ý*. The capital of *i* is a plain *I*.

blocks.title: Typing the marked letters
blocks.text: When you type an answer, a bar above the box offers *ä ç ž ň ö ş ü ý*, with a shift key for the capitals. An answer typed without the marks is shown the right spelling; in exercises about spelling it counts as wrong.

Turkmen spelling is regular. Each letter stands for one sound, and every letter is said: there are no silent letters, and an *e* at the end of a word is a full vowel (*täze*, new, has two syllables: tä-ze). Read a word letter by letter and you will be close. Six points need practice.

**y and ý are different letters.** *y* is a vowel. To make it, say “oo” and spread your lips instead of rounding them; it is close to the e of “roses”. *ý* is a consonant, the y of “yes”. A word can have both: *ýyl* (year) is ý, then the vowel y, then l.

items.note: *ý* is a consonant; the vowel is *o*
first the consonant *ý*, then the vowel *y*

blocks.title: A test for y and ý
blocks.text: Every syllable has exactly one vowel. If a *y* has a vowel right next to it (*aý*, *ýok*), it is the consonant *ý*. If it is the only vowel of its syllable (*gyz*, *gyzyl*), it is the vowel *y*.

**s and z.** Most Turkmen speakers say *s* and *z* with the tip of the tongue between the teeth, like the th of “thin” and the th of “this”: *salam* sounds close to “thalam”, and *göz* (eye) ends like “this”. You will also hear a plain s and z. Either way, they are spelled *s* and *z*.
**ň** is the sound at the end of “sing”, with no g after it: *meniň* (my) ends like “sing” without the g. It also comes in the middle of words: *teňňe* (a coin).
**ç and j.** *ç* is the ch of “church” and *j* the j of “jam”. They keep words apart: *çaý* is tea, *jaý* is a building.

**k and g beside a, o, u, y.** In words with these vowels, k and g are made further back in the mouth, near where you swallow: the k of *ýok* is deeper than the k of *kitap*, whose k comes before an i. Between two such vowels, g often softens into a breathy sound close to a French r, as in *aga* (older brother). Saying an English k and g is understood; this is what makes the accent.
**w** is made with the lips only, never with the teeth: *we* (and), *suw* (water). After a vowel at the end of a word, as in *suw*, it sounds like the w of “now”.

blocks.title: Don't add sounds
blocks.text: English spelling has taught you habits that Turkmen doesn't share. *ň* never has a g after it. A final *e* is never silent: *eje* (mother) is e-je. And *y* is never the y of “yes” on its own: that sound is always written *ý*.

sections.title: Long vowels, e and ä, and stress

blocks.text: Turkmen has short and long vowels, but the spelling doesn't show which is which. Most of the time you can say every vowel short and be understood. A few common words, though, are told apart only by the length of their vowel:
A long vowel is held about twice as long, as in “baa” against “bat”. Context nearly always tells you which word is meant: *Meniň adym Aýna* can only be about a name.

A long vowel also changes how a word takes endings. When an ending that starts with a vowel is added, a one-syllable word with a long vowel softens its last consonant: t becomes d. So *at* (name) gives *adym* (my name), but *at* (horse) gives *atym* (my horse). You will use *adym* and *adyň* in this unit as set phrases; the endings themselves come in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09).

items.note: two more words with a long vowel

blocks.text: **e and ä** are two different vowels, never two spellings of one sound. *e* is the e of “pet”. *ä* is more open, the a of “cat”. Each word has the one it has, and the meaning can depend on it, so learn the spelling with the word:
*neme* and *teze* are misspellings. If you are not sure whether a word has *e* or *ä*, check the word list of the lesson or a dictionary: you can't guess it from the sound of other words.
**Stress** usually falls on the last syllable: sa-LAM, ki-TAP, tä-ZE. When endings are added, they usually take the stress. Turkmen stress is light, so getting it wrong rarely blocks understanding.
Four facts explain most of what you will meet in the first units.
**Endings stack on a root.** Where English uses separate small words (in, my, the plural s), Turkmen adds endings, called suffixes, to the end of a word, one after another, each with one job:
**The verb comes last.** The usual order is subject, then object, then verb: *Men çaý içýärin*, literally “I tea drink”, means I drink tea. Endings on the verb show who does it (*-in*: I).
**No gender, no articles.** *ol* means he, she or it. There is no word for “the”, and *bir* (one) can work as “a”: *kitap* is a book or the book, as the context says.
**“To be” is often not said.** In the present, “I am”, “you are” and “he is” usually have no word at all: you put the two things side by side. That is how you introduce yourself:

items.en: He's a student. / She's a student.

items.note: the verb, with its ending, comes last

blocks.text: Read a long Turkmen word from the left: the root comes first and tells you what it is about; each ending then adds one piece of meaning. The guides show the pieces with a bar: *öý|ler|de*.

summary: Turkmen has 30 letters. Eight carry a mark (*ä, ç, ž, ň, ö, ş, ü, ý*), and each is a letter of its own; c, q, v and x are not used.
One letter, one sound, and every letter is said, including a final *e*.
*y* is a vowel (*gyz*), *ý* the consonant of “yes” (*ýok*); a *y* with a vowel beside it is *ý*.
*s* and *z* are usually said like the th of “thin” and “this”; *ň* is the ng of “sing”; *ç* is ch, *j* is j.
Long vowels aren't written: *at* is both “horse” and “name” (long a, so *adym*, my name).
Suffixes stack on a root, the verb comes last, there is no gender and no “the”, and “to be” is often left out: *Men Merdan*.
